# When an AI agent cannot run your tests

How I adapted tooling tests for a restricted environment, and why some checks still needed the real machine\.

By Mustafa Hafeez · 2026-11-10

## The takeaway

Before replacing an external dependency with a fixture, identify the real behaviour each test must still observe\.

![A paper model testing station inside a transparent enclosure and a physical computer feed results towards a shared review notebook\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/agent-test-environments-cover.webp)

A conceptual illustration of testing inside a restricted environment and against the real machine\.

## The agent could edit the code, but the tests were blocked

Some tests in my app’s developer tooling worked on the real machine and failed to run inside the coding agent’s sandbox\. They needed access to process lists and local sockets that the restricted environment could not provide\.

I wanted the agent to check useful parts of its work before handing a change back\. Sending every verification run outside the sandbox would leave another person or agent to do it\.

I chose to adapt the tests that could run inside, while keeping checks of real\-machine behaviour in a separate host run\. During review, we found that some replacements had lost behaviour the original tests checked\.

## Two questions were being tested together

Consider a tool that checks whether a background process is running\. It has to obtain a process list from the operating system, then decide whether the process it wants appears in that list\.

Those are two questions\. Can the tool make the right decision from the information it receives? And can it get the right information from the machine?

Supplied test data, often called a fixture, can answer the first question\. Give the code a known list and check its decision\. This can run inside a restricted environment without inspecting the laptop’s other processes\.

The second question needs access to the real interaction\. A supplied list cannot tell us whether the operating\-system command works\.

## What a fixture can show

This teaching example uses invented process identifiers\. The function receives another function, listProcesses, which supplies the list\. That lets a test control the input without asking the operating system\.

```
function isRunning(pid, listProcesses) {
  return listProcesses().includes(pid);
}

isRunning(42, () => [42, 73]); // true
isRunning(42, () => [73]);     // false
```

## The real command could break while those tests passed

In the first call, the supplied list contains 42, so isRunning returns true\. The second list contains only 73, so it returns false\. Together they check the present and absent decisions\.

Both would keep passing if the real process\-list command stopped working\. Neither call uses it\. That missing interaction needs its own check, for example by starting a controlled process and verifying that the real observation can find it\.

There is another question to settle when reviewing code like this\. What happens if the process list is unavailable? Returning an empty list would make an observation failure look like an absent process\. The implementation needs an explicit way to handle that uncertainty\. This is a review question, rather than a further bug found in my tooling\.

## Review found what the replacements could no longer see

One replacement test asserted information it had constructed itself\. Another could only see processes it had already been told about, so a stray process could escape its view\.

Those findings changed the repair\. The original operating\-system checks were preserved in a separately named host\-only set\. Fixture\-based tests covered the decisions inside the sandbox\.

The comparison that helped was to ask what each old test observed and what its replacement could observe\. A similar assertion or a passing test count would have missed that difference\.

![Use sandbox fixtures to test decisions from known inputs\. Keep host integration checks for real system interactions\. Review both results\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/agent-test-environments-flow-v2.svg)

Fixture and host checks answer separate questions about the same implementation\.

## Both test runs needed a result

The recorded final checks passed for the targeted sandbox suites and the full host run\. Each result had a different scope\. The sandbox tests covered the selected decisions using controlled inputs, and the host run supplied the broader integration evidence\.

Keeping host checks separate creates an ongoing job\. They need a clear place in the review process, otherwise a move intended to make tests runnable can quietly leave some checks behind\.

A useful handover identifies which tests ran, where they ran, the revision and the result\. If a sandbox run excludes host\-only tests, its result needs the corresponding host result alongside it\.

## Ask what the test actually observes

Before replacing a dependency in a test, write down what the existing test can see\. Then ask whether the implementation could break while the replacement still passed\. Identify the check that would catch that failure and where it will run\.

A database gives another example\. A fake returned row can help test how code handles the data\. A separate integration test can establish whether the real query and connection work in the intended environment\.

In my tooling, fixtures made decision tests runnable inside the sandbox\. Keeping the host checks preserved the evidence about real process behaviour that the fixtures could not supply\.

## About this note

Based on my work adapting developer\-tooling tests for a restricted environment\. Implementation details are generalised, and the code example uses invented identifiers\.

## Sources

- [Jest documentation on replacing dependencies with mock data](<https://jestjs.io/docs/manual-mocks>)

[Read on the website](https://mustafahafeez.com/blog/tests-inside-agent-sandbox/)


# Before I accept an AI agent’s changes

Checking what my website build would publish, and how I tested an AI agent’s release check\.

By Mustafa Hafeez · 2026-11-09

## The takeaway

Choose one failure the change must reject, demonstrate that rejection, and attach the result to the version being released\.

![Conceptual paper models of an app and websites bring work towards a human review desk and release gate\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/ai-agent-review-cover.webp)

A conceptual illustration of preparing work across an app and its websites\.

## A successful build left a question

While building this website with AI coding agents, I needed to keep drafts, build scripts and agent instructions private\. The finished pages belonged in a public repository\. The source belonged in a separate private one\.

A successful build could still copy an unwanted file into the public output\. Looking at the website in a browser would tell me whether the pages looked right\. It would leave a stray notes file sitting alongside those pages unseen\.

Agents helped implement the publishing checks\. Before accepting that work, I wanted to see what happened when the output contained something that had no reason to go live\.

## An approved list gave me something to compare

The build writes the public website into its own output directory\. The checker walks that directory, lists every file and compares the result with the files approved for release\. An unexpected file or a missing one stops the check\.

The complete inventory matters\. A list of forbidden names only covers names someone has thought of\. A new notes file could have any name\. And a check that only visits the approved files would never discover an extra one\.

This small JavaScript example shows the comparison with invented filenames\. The real checker also handles symbolic links and other release checks\.

```
const approved = new Set(['index.html', 'assets/site.css']);
const actual = ['index.html', 'assets/site.css', 'notes.txt'];

const unexpected = actual.filter(file => !approved.has(file));
const missing = [...approved].filter(file => !actual.includes(file));

if (unexpected.length || missing.length) {
  throw new Error('Output differs from approved file list');
}
```

![Build a clean output folder, list every file and compare with the approved list\. Stop on a mismatch\. A match proceeds to remaining release checks\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/release-file-check-flow-v2.svg)

The file inventory is one release check\. Matching filenames still need content and credential checks\.

## I added a file that should be rejected

For this article, I copied the current build into a temporary directory and checked the clean copy\. Then I added a harmless file called editorial\-notes\.txt at its root and ran the same checker again\.

I put it outside the reserved private folders so the test would reach the approved\-list comparison\. Otherwise a separate private\-folder rule might reject it first, leaving the comparison untested\.

The clean copy passed\. The copy containing the extra file failed\. These were the recorded results\.

```
Clean output accepted
Deploy artifact differs from positive allowlist
```

## What that result established

The check rejected the extra file in that temporary copy\. That gave me evidence about the behaviour I had asked the agents to implement\.

The short JavaScript example reaches the same kind of failure because notes\.txt appears in actual but not in approved\. Remove that extra filename and both lists match\. The code teaches the comparison\. The temporary\-directory check exercised the website’s actual checker\.

If a checker accepted the unwanted file, I would look at how it collected the inventory and whether a mismatch stopped publication\. If the checker rejected it but the build kept copying it, the copy step would need fixing\. Adding the file to the approved list just to get a pass would hide the problem\.

The approved list still needs maintenance\. When I deliberately add a public page or image, I update it as part of reviewing what will become public\.

## The result has to follow the release

I record the source revision checked and publish the reviewed output manually\. If an agent changes the build afterwards, the changed output needs checking again\. An earlier result describes the earlier version\.

After publication, I compare the local public text files with the files served by the website\. That answers a different question\. A correct build can be ready locally while the host still serves an older copy\.

The file inventory has a limit too\. A JavaScript file can have an approved name and still contain private information\. Content review, credential scanning and browser checks each cover further parts of the release\.

![Tests and review match revision A\. A later edit creates revision B, which needs its own review before release\.](https://mustafahafeez.com/assets/images/articles/ai-agent-revision-evidence-v4.webp)

A simplified illustration\. Evidence recorded for revision A does not establish that revision B has been checked\.

## A check to try on your next change

Choose one unwanted outcome the change must prevent\. Prepare an input that should trigger it, run the check and inspect what actually happened\. Keep the result with the version you checked\.

The same approach could help with a data pipeline\. Give it a sample with a required field missing, then inspect the published report as well as the job status\. A failure message would leave a problem if malformed data had already reached the report\. This is a suggested application, rather than an incident from my work\.

For this website, the useful evidence was straightforward\. The same checker accepted the clean copy and rejected the copy containing an unapproved file\.

## About this note

Based on my personal website’s publishing checks\. The rejection result came from a temporary copy containing a harmless fixture\. The code is a simplified illustration with invented filenames\.

[Read on the website](https://mustafahafeez.com/blog/reviewing-ai-agent-work/)
